Neonatal Eurasian elk enter the world at a substantial mass, with newborns typically weighing around 12,844 grams [Wwb = around 12,844 grams]. This considerable birth weight is characteristic of a precocial ungulate adapted to cool boreal environments. The gestation period supporting this development lasts 243 days [tg = 243 days], a duration measured at a core body temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C], which is typical for a large mammal. This lengthy intrauterine development ensures that the calf is born at an advanced stage, capable of standing and following its mother within hours. The high birth mass is also an investment in neonatal survival, as a larger calf is better insulated against the cold. Weaning from maternal milk occurs relatively early in the life history of the elk, with nutritional independence being achieved after a period of about 100 days following birth [tx = about 100 days following birth], again at 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C]. By this time, the calf has reached a wet weight of 94,000 grams [Wwx = 94,000 grams], having more than septupled its birth weight through rapid post-natal growth fueled by rich maternal milk.

The transition to reproductive maturity in Eurasian elk is a prolonged process, reflecting their position as a large, long-lived herbivore. Puberty is not reached until approximately 751 days after birth [tp = approximately 751 days after birth], a developmental milestone timed under the standard mammalian body temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C]. This delayed maturation is common among cervids of significant body size, as substantial energy must be directed toward structural growth and the accumulation of body reserves before gametogenesis can commence. The time invested in somatic development ultimately influences the dually dimorphic nature of the species' adult body size. Females achieve an asymptotic or ultimate wet weight of approximately 360,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 360,000 grams], with field records showing a range from 200 up to 490 kilograms. This considerable mass is supported by a high daily energy intake during peak foraging seasons. For a female at 360 kilograms, the measured energy intake required to sustain her metabolism and activity is 40.9 megajoules per day , a figure that highlights the immense foraging pressure these animals place on their habitat.

Male Eurasian elk far outstrip females in ultimate body size, attaining an asymptotic wet weight of approximately 520,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 520,000 grams]. Reports from managed populations indicate this can range from 380 up to 700 kilograms, making the bull elk one of the largest living terrestrial mammals in the Northern Hemisphere. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism is a direct consequence of a polygynous mating system, where larger males have a distinct advantage in the intense rutting competitions for access to females. The massive energy requirements of a bull at this scale are substantial, but the most critical energetic bottleneck occurs for females during gestation and early lactation. The maximum reproductive rate for this species is realized only under exceptional nutritional conditions. When food is abundant, a cow may produce two calves per year, corresponding to an annual output of about 1.3 calves per year [Ri = about 1.3 calves per year], though in most years a single calf is the norm.

The maximum lifespan of the Eurasian elk in the wild is a subject of considerable ecological interest, with the oldest documented individuals reaching an age of approximately 25 years [am = approximately 25 years] at a temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C]. This upper ceiling of longevity, measured at a body temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C], places the elk among the longer-lived of the cervids, a status partly attributable to the low predation risk faced by large adults in most of their current range, where wolves and bears are the primary natural predators. Attaining such an age requires the animal to survive the considerable energetic deficits of multiple harsh winters and the physiological stress of annual breeding seasons. The life table of a natural population shows that mortality is quite high for calves and juveniles, but it becomes relatively low and stable for prime-aged adults before rising again due to senescence after about 15 years. This extended reproductive window allows a single productive female to contribute several litters of calves over her lifetime, though the interval between births is typically one or two years given the demands of lactation.

Seasonal foraging strategies in Eurasian elk are tightly linked to their massive energetic demands, particularly the requirement to deposit fat reserves for winter survival. During the summer, individuals must increase their food intake dramatically to meet the daily energetic needs of lactation, antler growth, and body mass gain. The peak ingestion rate is impressive; for a 360-kilogram animal, the maximum daily food intake has been measured at 40.9 megajoules per day , a value derived from observation of feeding rates on high-quality browse such as willow and birch. As summer advances, the young calf, which began life at over twelve thousand grams (12,844 grams) [Wwb = 12,844 grams], continues its rapid growth until weaning. By the time the mother ceases lactation, the weanling has attained a robust mass of 94,000 grams [Wwx = 94,000 grams]. This substantial body size is critical as the juvenile must survive its first winter on its own, relying on the fat stores and foraging skills it has developed under maternal guidance during the preceding 100 days [tx = 100 days] of dependency at a temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C].
